arXiv:1410.1441v2 [quant-ph] 19 Nov 2014

Fidelity of recovery and geometric squashed entanglement

Kaushik P. Seshadreesan ††thanks: Hearne Institute for Theoretical Physics, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana 70803, USA    Mark M. Wilde11footnotemark: 1 ††thanks: Center for Computation and Technology, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana 70803, USA
Abstract

This paper defines the fidelity of recovery of a tripartite quantum state on systems AA, BB, and CC as a measure of how well one can recover the full state on all three systems if system AA is lost and a recovery operation is performed on system CC alone. The surprisal of the fidelity of recovery (its negative logarithm) is an information quantity which obeys nearly all of the properties of the conditional quantum mutual information I⁡(A;B|C)I(A;B|C), including non-negativity, monotonicity under local operations, duality, and a dimension bound. We then define an entanglement measure based on this quantity, which we call the geometric squashed entanglement. We prove that the geometric squashed entanglement is an entanglement monotone, that it vanishes if and only if the state on which it is evaluated is unentangled, and that it reduces to the geometric measure of entanglement if the state is pure. We also show that it is subadditive, continuous, and normalized on maximally entangled states. We next define the surprisal of measurement recovery fidelity, which is an information quantity in the spirit of quantum discord, characterizing how well one can recover a share of a bipartite state if it is measured. We prove that this discord-like quantity satisfies several properties, including non-negativity, faithfulness on classical-quantum states, invariance under local isometries, dimension bounds, and normalization on maximally entangled states. This quantity combined with a recent breakthrough of Fawzi and Renner allows to characterize states with discord nearly equal to zero as being approximate fixed points of entanglement breaking channels (equivalently, they are recoverable from the state of a measuring apparatus). Finally, we discuss a multipartite fidelity of recovery and several of its properties.

1 Introduction

The conditional quantum mutual information (CQMI) is a central information quantity that finds numerous applications in quantum information theory [DY08, YD09], the theory of quantum correlations [OZ01, CW04], and quantum many-body physics [Kim13b, Bas12]. For a quantum state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} shared between three parties, say, Alice, Bob, and Charlie, the CQMI is defined as

I​(A;B|C)ρ≡H​(A​C)ρ+H​(B​C)ρ−H​(C)ρ−H​(A​B​C)ρ,I(A;B|C)_{\rho}\equiv H(AC)_{\rho}+H(BC)_{\rho}-H(C)_{\rho}-H(ABC)_{\rho}, (1.1)

where H(F)σ≡−H(F)_{\sigma}\equiv-Tr{σF​log⁡σF}\{\sigma_{F}\log\sigma_{F}\} is the von Neumann entropy of a state σF\sigma_{F} on system FF and we unambiguously let ρC≡\rho_{C}\equiv\ Tr{ρA​B​C}A​B{}_{AB}\{\rho_{ABC}\} denote the reduced density operator on system CC, for example. The CQMI captures the correlations present between Alice and Bob from the perspective of Charlie in the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) resource limit, where an asymptotically large number of copies of the state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} are shared between the three parties. It is non-negative [LR73a, LR73b], non-increasing under the action of local quantum operations on systems AA or BB, and obeys a duality relation for a four-party pure state ψA​B​C​D\psi_{ABCD}, given by I​(A;B|C)ψ=I​(B;A|D)ψI(A;B|C)_{\psi}=I(B;A|D)_{\psi}. It finds operational meaning as the optimal quantum communication cost in the i.i.d. state redistribution protocol [DY08, YD09]. It underlies the squashed entanglement [CW04], which is a measure of entanglement that satisfies all of the axioms desired for such a measure [AF04, KW04, BCY11], and furthermore underlies the quantum discord [OZ01], which is a measure of quantum correlations different from those due to entanglement.

In an attempt to develop a version of the CQMI, which would be relevant for the “one-shot” or finite resource regimes, we along with Berta [BSW14] recently proposed Rényi generalizations of the CQMI. We proved that these Rényi generalizations of the CQMI retain many of the properties of the original CQMI in (1.1). While the application of these particular Rényi CQMIs in one-shot state redistribution remains to be studied,11 1 However, see the recent progress on one-shot state redistribution in [BCT14, DHO14]. we have used them to define a Rényi squashed entanglement and a Rényi quantum discord [SBW14], which retain several properties of the respective, original, von Neumann entropy based quantities.

One contribution of [BSW14] was the conjecture that the proposed Rényi CQMIs are monotone increasing in the Rényi parameter, as is known to be the case for other Rényi entropic quantities. That is, for a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, and for a Rényi conditional mutual information I~α​(A;B|C)ρ\widetilde{I}_{\alpha}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho} defined as [BSW14, Section 6]

I~α​(A;B|C)ρ≡1α−1​log⁡‖ρA​B​C1/2​ρA​C(1−α)/2​α​ρC(α−1)/2​α​ρB​C(1−α)/2​α‖2​α2​α,\widetilde{I}_{\alpha}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\equiv\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\left\|\rho_{ABC}^{1/2}\rho_{AC}^{(1-\alpha)/2\alpha}\rho_{C}^{(\alpha-1)/2\alpha}\rho_{BC}^{(1-\alpha)/2\alpha}\right\|_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha}, (1.2)

[BSW14, Section 8] conjectured that the following inequality holds for 0≤α≤β0\leq\alpha\leq\beta:

I~α​(A;B|C)ρ≤I~β​(A;B|C)ρ.\widetilde{I}_{\alpha}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\leq\widetilde{I}_{\beta}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}. (1.3)

Proofs were given for this conjectured inequality when the Rényi parameter α\alpha is in a neighborhood of one and when 1/α+1/β=21/\alpha+1/\beta=2 [BSW14, Section 8].

We also pointed out implications of the conjectured inequality for understanding states with small conditional quantum mutual information [BSW14, Section 8] (later stressed in [Ber14]). In particular, we pointed out that the following lower bound on the conditional quantum mutual information holds as a consequence of the conjectured inequality in (1.3) by choosing α=1/2\alpha=1/2 and β=1\beta=1:

I​(A;B|C)ρ\displaystyle I\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho} ≥−log⁡F⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛC→A​CP​(ρB​C))\displaystyle\geq-\log F\left(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{P}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right) (1.4)
≥14​‖ρA​B​C−ℛC→A​CP​(ρB​C)‖12,\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{4}\left\|\rho_{ABC}-\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{P}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right\|_{1}^{2}, (1.5)

where ℛC→A​CP\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{P} is a quantum channel known as the Petz recovery map [HJPW04], defined as

ℛC→A​CP(⋅)≡ρA​C1/2ρC−1/2(⋅)ρC−1/2ρA​C1/2.\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{P}(\cdot)\equiv\rho_{AC}^{1/2}\rho_{C}^{-1/2}(\cdot)\rho_{C}^{-1/2}\rho_{AC}^{1/2}. (1.6)

The fidelity is a measure of how close two quantum states are and is defined for positive semidefinite operators PP and QQ as

F⁡(P,Q)≡‖P​Q‖12.F\left(P,Q\right)\equiv\left\|\sqrt{P}\sqrt{Q}\right\|_{1}^{2}. (1.7)

The trace distance bound in (1.4) was conjectured previously in [Kim13a] and a related conjecture (with a different lower bound) was considered in [WL12].

The conjectured inequality in (1.4) revealed that (if it is true) it would be possible to understand tripartite states with small conditional mutual information in the following sense: If one loses system AA of a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} and is allowed to perform the Petz recovery map on system CC alone, then the fidelity of recovery in doing so will be high. The converse statement was already established in [BSW14, Proposition 35] and independently in [FR14, Eq. (8)]. Indeed, suppose now that a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} has large conditional mutual information. Then if one loses system AA and attempts to recover it by acting on system CC alone, then the fidelity of recovery will not be high no matter what scheme is employed (see [BSW14, Proposition 35] for specific parameters). These statements are already known to be true for a classical system CC, but the main question is whether the inequality in (1.4) holds for a quantum system CC.

2 Summary of results

When studying the conjectured inequality in (1.4), we can observe that a simple lower bound on the RHS is in terms of a quantity that we call the surprisal of the fidelity of recovery:

−log⁡F⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛC→A​CP​(ρB​C))≥IF​(A;B|C)ρ≡−log⁡F​(A;B|C)ρ,-\log F\left(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{P}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right)\geq I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\equiv-\log F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}, (2.1)

where the fidelity of recovery is defined as

F​(A;B|C)ρ≡supℛF⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛC→A​C​(ρB​C)).F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\equiv\sup_{\mathcal{R}}F\left(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right). (2.2)

That is, rather than considering the particular Petz recovery map, one could consider optimizing the fidelity with respect to all such recovery maps. One of the main objectives of the present paper is to study the fidelity of recovery in more detail.22 2 Note: After the completion of this work, we learned of the recent breakthrough result of [FR14], in which the inequality I​(A;B|C)ρ≥−log⁡F​(A;B|C)ρI(A;B|C)_{\rho}\geq-\log F(A;B|C)_{\rho} was established for any tripartite state ρA​B​C∈𝒮⁡(ℋA⊗ℋB⊗ℋC)\rho_{ABC}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{C}). Thus, for states with small conditional mutual information (near to zero), the fidelity of recovery is high (near to one).

2.1 Properties of the surprisal of the fidelity of recovery

Our conclusions for IF​(A;B|C)ρI_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho} are that it obeys many of the same properties as the conditional mutual information I​(A;B|C)ρI\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}:

  1. 1.

    (Non-negativity) IF​(A;B|C)ρ≥0I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\geq 0 for any tripartite quantum state. (This one is obvious because the fidelity between two quantum states is bounded from above by one.)

  2. 2.

    (Monotonicity) IF​(A;B|C)ρI_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho} is monotone under quantum operations on systems AA and BB, in the sense that

    IF​(A;B|C)ρ≥IF​(A′;B′|C)ω,I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\geq I_{F}\left(A^{\prime};B^{\prime}|C\right)_{\omega}, (2.3)

    where ωA​B​C≡(𝒩A→A′⊗ℳB→B′)​(ρA​B​C)\omega_{ABC}\equiv\left(\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\right)\left(\rho_{ABC}\right) and 𝒩A→A′\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}} and ℳB→B′\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}} are quantum channels acting on systems AA and BB, respectively.

  3. 3.

    (Duality) For a four-party pure state ψA​B​C​D\psi_{ABCD}, the following duality relation holds

    IF​(A;B|C)ψ=IF​(A;B|D)ψ.I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\psi}=I_{F}\left(A;B|D\right)_{\psi}. (2.4)
  4. 4.

    (Dimension bound) The following dimension bound holds

    IF​(A;B|C)ψ≤2​log⁡|A|,I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\psi}\leq 2\log\left|A\right|, (2.5)

    where |A|\left|A\right| is the dimension of the system AA.

  5. 5.

    (Weak chain rule) The chain rule for conditional mutual information of a four-party state ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD} is as follows:

    I​(A​C;B|D)ρ=I​(A;B|C​D)ρ+I​(C;B|D)ρ.I\left(AC;B|D\right)_{\rho}=I\left(A;B|CD\right)_{\rho}+I\left(C;B|D\right)_{\rho}. (2.6)

    We find something weaker than this for IFI_{F}, which we call the weak chain rule for IFI_{F}:

    IF​(A​C;B|D)ρ≥IF​(A;B|C​D)ρ.I_{F}\left(AC;B|D\right)_{\rho}\geq I_{F}\left(A;B|CD\right)_{\rho}. (2.7)

2.2 Geometric squashed entanglement

Our next contribution is to define an entanglement measure of a bipartite state that we call the geometric squashed entanglement. To motivate this quantity, recall that the squashed entanglement of a bipartite state ρA​B\rho_{AB} is defined as

Esq​(A,B)ρ≡12​infωA​B​E{I​(A;B|E)ω:ρA​B=TrE⁡{ωA​B​E}},E^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\inf_{\omega_{ABE}}\left\{I\left(A;B|E\right)_{\omega}:\rho_{AB}=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}\left\{\omega_{ABE}\right\}\right\}, (2.8)

where the infimum is over all extensions ωA​B​E\omega_{ABE} of the state ρA​B\rho_{AB} [CW04]. The interpretation of Esq​(A,B)ρE^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho} is that it quantifies the correlations present between Alice and Bob after a third party (often associated to an environment or eavesdropper) attempts to “squash down” their correlations. In light of the above discussion, we define the geometric squashed entanglement simply by replacing the conditional mutual information with IFI_{F}:

EFsq​(A,B)ρ≡12​infωA​B​E{IF​(A;B|E)ω:ρA​B=TrE⁡{ωA​B​E}}.E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\inf_{\omega_{ABE}}\left\{I_{F}\left(A;B|E\right)_{\omega}:\rho_{AB}=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}\left\{\omega_{ABE}\right\}\right\}. (2.9)

We also employ the related quantity throughout the paper:

Fsq​(A,B)ρ≡supωA​B​E{F​(A;B|E)ρ:ρA​B=TrE⁡{ωA​B​E}},F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\equiv\sup_{\omega_{ABE}}\left\{F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\rho}:\rho_{AB}=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}\left\{\omega_{ABE}\right\}\right\}, (2.10)

with the two of them being related by

EFsq​(A,B)ρ=−12​log⁡Fsq​(A,B)ρ.E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}=-\frac{1}{2}\log F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}. (2.11)

We prove the following results for the geometric squashed entanglement, justifying it as an entanglement measure in its own right:

  1. 1.

    (Entanglement Monotone) The geometric squashed entanglement of ρA​B\rho_{AB} does not increase under local operations and classical communication. That is, the following inequality holds

    EFsq​(A,B)ρ≥EFsq​(A′,B′)ω,E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\geq E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A^{\prime};B^{\prime}\right)_{\omega}, (2.12)

    where ωA​B≡ΛA​B→A′​B′​(ρA​B)\omega_{AB}\equiv\Lambda_{AB\rightarrow A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}\left(\rho_{AB}\right) and ΛA​B→A′​B′\Lambda_{AB\rightarrow A^{\prime}B^{\prime}} is a quantum channel realized by local operations and classical communication. The geometric squashed entanglement is also convex, i.e.,

    ∑xpX​(x)​EFsq​(A,B)ρx≥EFsq​(A,B)ρ¯,\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho^{x}}\geq E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\overline{\rho}}, (2.13)

    where

    ρ¯A​B≡∑xpX​(x)​ρA​Bx.\overline{\rho}_{AB}\equiv\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\rho_{AB}^{x}. (2.14)
  2. 2.

    (Faithfulness) The geometric squashed entanglement of ρA​B\rho_{AB} is equal to zero if and only if ρA​B\rho_{AB} is a separable (unentangled) state. In particular, we prove the following bound by appealing directly to the argument in [WL12]:

    EFsq​(A,B)ρ≥1512​|A|4​‖ρA​B−SEP​(A:B)‖14,E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\geq\frac{1}{512\left|A\right|^{4}}\left\|\rho_{AB}-\text{SEP}(A:B)\right\|_{1}^{4}, (2.15)

    where the trace distance to separable states is defined by

    ‖ρA​B−SEP(A:B)‖1≡infσA​B∈SEP​(A:B)‖ρA​B−σA​B‖1.\left\|\rho_{AB}-\text{SEP}(A:B)\right\|_{1}\equiv\inf_{\sigma_{AB}\in\text{SEP}\left(A:B\right)}\left\|\rho_{AB}-\sigma_{AB}\right\|_{1}. (2.16)
  3. 3.

    (Reduction to geometric measure) The geometric squashed entanglement of a pure state |ϕ⟩A​B\left|\phi\right\rangle_{AB} reduces to a variant of the well known geometric measure of entanglement [WG03] (see also [CAH14] and references therein):

    EFsq(A;B)ψ=−12logsup|φ⟩A⟨ϕ|A​B(φA⊗ϕB)|ϕ⟩A​BE_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\psi}=-\frac{1}{2}\log\sup_{\left|\varphi\right\rangle_{A}}\left\langle\phi\right|_{AB}\left(\varphi_{A}\otimes\phi_{B}\right)\left|\phi\right\rangle_{AB} (2.17)
  4. 4.

    (Normalization) The geometric squashed entanglement of a maximally entangled state ΦA​B\Phi_{AB} is equal to log⁡d\log d, where dd is the Schmidt rank of ΦA​B\Phi_{AB}. It is larger than log⁡d\log d when evaluated for a private state [HHHO05, HHHO09] of log⁡d\log d private bits.

  5. 5.

    (Subadditivity) The geometric squashed entanglement is subadditive for tensor-product states, i.e.,

    EFsq​(A1​A2,B1​B2)ω≤EFsq​(A1,B1)ρ+EFsq​(A2,B2)σ,E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A_{1}A_{2};B_{1}B_{2}\right)_{\omega}\leq E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A_{1};B_{1}\right)_{\rho}+E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A_{2};B_{2}\right)_{\sigma}, (2.18)

    where ωA1​B1​A2​B2≡ρA1​B1⊗σA2​B2\omega_{A_{1}B_{1}A_{2}B_{2}}\equiv\rho_{A_{1}B_{1}}\otimes\sigma_{A_{2}B_{2}}.

  6. 6.

    (Continuity) If two quantum states ρA​B\rho_{AB} and σA​B\sigma_{AB} are close in trace distance, then their respective geometric squashed entanglements are close as well.

2.3 Surprisal of measurement recovery fidelity

The quantum discord D​(A¯,B)ρD\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho} is an information quantity which characterizes quantum correlations of a bipartite state ρA​B\rho_{AB}, by quantifying how much correlation is lost through the act of a quantum measurement [OZ01] (we give a full definition later on). By a chain of reasoning detailed in Section 6, we define the surprisal of measurement recovery fidelity of a bipartite state as follows:

DF(A¯;B)ρ≡−logsupℰAF(ρA​B,ℰA(ρA​B)),D_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho}\equiv-\log\sup_{\mathcal{E}_{A}}F\left(\rho_{AB},\mathcal{E}_{A}\left(\rho_{AB}\right)\right),

where the supremum is over the convex set of entanglement breaking channels [HSR03]. Since every entanglement breaking channel can be written as a concatenation of a measurement map followed by a preparation map, DF​(A¯,B)ρD_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho} characterizes how well one can recover a bipartite state after performing a quantum measurement on one share of it. Equivalently, the quantity captures how close ρA​B\rho_{AB} is to being a fixed point of an entanglement breaking channel.

We establish several properties of DF​(A¯,B)ρD_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho}, which are analogous to properties known to hold for the quantum discord [MBC+12]:

  1. 1.

    (Non-negativity) This follows trivially because the fidelity between two quantum states is always a real number between zero and one.

  2. 2.

    (Invariance under local isometries) DF​(A¯,B)ρD_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho} is invariant under local isometries, in the sense that

    DF​(A¯,B)ρ=DF​(A′¯,B′)σ,D_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho}=D_{F}(\overline{A^{\prime}};B^{\prime})_{\sigma}, (2.19)

    where

    σA′​B′≡(𝒰A→A′⊗𝒱B→B′)​(ρA​B)\sigma_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}\equiv\left(\mathcal{U}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{V}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\right)\left(\rho_{AB}\right) (2.20)

    and 𝒰A→A′\mathcal{U}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}} and 𝒱B→B′\mathcal{V}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}} are isometric quantum channels.

  3. 3.

    (Faithfulness) DF​(A¯,B)ρD_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho} is equal to zero if and only if ρA​B\rho_{AB} is a classical-quantum state (classical on system AA).

  4. 4.

    (Dimension bound) DF​(A¯,B)ρ≤2​log⁡|A|D_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho}\leq 2\log\left|A\right|.

  5. 5.

    (Normalization) DF​(A¯,B)ΦD_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\Phi} for a maximally entangled state ΦA​B\Phi_{AB} is equal to log⁡d\log d, where dd is the Schmidt rank of ΦA​B\Phi_{AB}.

  6. 6.

    (Monotonicity) The suprisal of measurement recovery fidelity is monotone with respect to quantum operations on the unmeasured system, i.e.,

    DF​(A¯,B)ρ≥DF​(A¯,B′)σ,D_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho}\geq D_{F}\left(\overline{A};B^{\prime}\right)_{\sigma}, (2.21)

    where σA​B′≡𝒩B→B′​(ρA​B)\sigma_{AB^{\prime}}\equiv\mathcal{N}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\left(\rho_{AB}\right).

  7. 7.

    (Continuity) If two quantum states ρA​B\rho_{AB} and σA​B\sigma_{AB} are close in trace distance, then the respective DF​(A¯,B)D_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right) quantities are close as well.

Finally, we use DF​(A¯,B)ρD_{F}\left(\overline{A};B\right)_{\rho} and a recent result of Fawzi and Renner [FR14] to establish that the quantum discord of ρA​B\rho_{AB} is nearly equal to zero if and only if ρA​B\rho_{AB} is an approximate fixed point of entanglement breaking channel (i.e., if it is possible to nearly recover ρA​B\rho_{AB} after performing a measurement on the system AA).

3 Preliminaries

Norms, states, extensions, channels, and measurements. Let ℬ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}\right) denote the algebra of bounded linear operators acting on a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}. We restrict ourselves to finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces throughout this paper. For α≥1\alpha\geq 1, we define the α\alpha-norm of an operator XX as

‖X‖α≡Tr⁡{(X†​X)α}1/α.\left\|X\right\|_{\alpha}\equiv\operatorname{Tr}\{(\sqrt{X^{{\dagger}}X})^{\alpha}\}^{1/\alpha}. (3.1)

Let ℬ​(ℋ)+\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}\right)_{+} denote the subset of positive semi-definite operators. We also write X≥0X\geq 0 if X∈ℬ​(ℋ)+X\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}\right)_{+}. An operator ρ\rho is in the set 𝒮⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{S}\left(\mathcal{H}\right) of density operators (or states) if ρ∈ℬ​(ℋ)+\rho\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}\right)_{+} and Tr{ρ}=1\left\{\rho\right\}=1. The tensor product of two Hilbert spaces ℋA\mathcal{H}_{A} and ℋB\mathcal{H}_{B} is denoted by ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B} or ℋA​B\mathcal{H}_{AB}. Given a multipartite density operator ρA​B∈𝒮⁡(ℋA⊗ℋB)\rho_{AB}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}), we unambiguously write ρA=\rho_{A}=\ Tr{ρA​B}B{}_{B}\left\{\rho_{AB}\right\} for the reduced density operator on system AA. We use ρA​B\rho_{AB}, σA​B\sigma_{AB}, τA​B\tau_{AB}, ωA​B\omega_{AB}, etc. to denote general density operators in 𝒮⁡(ℋA⊗ℋB)\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}), while ψA​B\psi_{AB}, φA​B\varphi_{AB}, ϕA​B\phi_{AB}, etc. denote rank-one density operators (pure states) in 𝒮⁡(ℋA⊗ℋB)\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}) (with it implicit, clear from the context, and the above convention implying that ψA\psi_{A}, φA\varphi_{A}, ϕA\phi_{A} are mixed if ψA​B\psi_{AB}, φA​B\varphi_{AB}, ϕA​B\phi_{AB} are pure and entangled).

We also say that pure-state vectors |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle in ℋ\mathcal{H} are states. Any bipartite pure state |ψ⟩A​B|\psi\rangle_{AB} in ℋA​B\mathcal{H}_{AB} is written in Schmidt form as

|ψ⟩A​B≡∑i=0d−1λi|i⟩A|i⟩B,\left|\psi\right\rangle_{AB}\equiv\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}\left|i\right\rangle_{A}\left|i\right\rangle_{B}, (3.2)

where {|i⟩A}\{|i\rangle_{A}\} and {|i⟩B}\{|i\rangle_{B}\} form orthonormal bases in ℋA\mathcal{H}_{A} and ℋB\mathcal{H}_{B}, respectively, dd is the Schmidt rank of the state, and ∑i=0d−1λi=1\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\lambda_{i}=1. By a maximally entangled state, we mean a bipartite pure state of the form

|Φ⟩A​B≡1d∑i=0d−1|i⟩A|i⟩B.\left|\Phi\right\rangle_{AB}\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\left|i\right\rangle_{A}\left|i\right\rangle_{B}. (3.3)

A state γA​B​A′​B′\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}} is a private state [HHHO05, HHHO09] if Alice and Bob can extract a secret key from it by performing local von Neumann measurements on the AA and BB systems of γA​B​A′​B′\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}, such that the resulting secret key is product with any purifying system of γA​B​A′​B′\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}. The systems A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime} are known as “shield systems” because they aid in keeping the key secure from any eavesdropper possessing the purifying system. Interestingly, a private state of log⁡d\log d private bits can be written in the following form [HHHO05, HHHO09]:

γA​B​A′​B′=UA​B​A′​B′​(ΦA​B⊗ρA′​B′)​UA​B​A′​B′†,\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}=U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}\left(\Phi_{AB}\otimes\rho_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}\right)U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{{\dagger}}, (3.4)

where

UA​B​A′​B′=∑i,j|i⟩⟨i|A⊗|j⟩⟨j|B⊗UA′​B′i​j.U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}=\sum_{i,j}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle i\right|_{A}\otimes\left|j\right\rangle\left\langle j\right|_{B}\otimes U_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{ij}. (3.5)

The unitaries can be chosen such that UA′​B′i​j=VA′​B′jU_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{ij}=V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{j} or UA′​B′i​j=VA′​B′iU_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{ij}=V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}. This implies that the unitary UA​B​A′​B′U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}} can be implemented either as

UA​B​A′​B′=∑i|i⟩⟨i|A⊗IB⊗VA′​B′iU_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}=\sum_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle i\right|_{A}\otimes I_{B}\otimes V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i} (3.6)

or

UA​B​A′​B′=IA⊗∑i|i⟩⟨i|B⊗VA′​B′i.U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}=I_{A}\otimes\sum_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle i\right|_{B}\otimes V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}. (3.7)

The trace distance between two quantum states ρ,σ∈𝒮⁡(ℋ)\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal{S}\left(\mathcal{H}\right) is equal to ‖ρ−σ‖1\left\|\rho-\sigma\right\|_{1}. It has a direct operational interpretation in terms of the distinguishability of these states. That is, if ρ\rho or σ\sigma are prepared with equal probability and the task is to distinguish them via some quantum measurement, then the optimal success probability in doing so is equal to (1+‖ρ−σ‖1/2)/2\left(1+\left\|\rho-\sigma\right\|_{1}/2\right)/2.

A linear map 𝒩A→B:ℬ⁡(ℋA)→ℬ⁡(ℋB)\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow B}:\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}_{A}\right)\rightarrow\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}_{B}\right) is positive if 𝒩A→B​(σA)∈ℬ​(ℋB)+\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow B}\left(\sigma_{A}\right)\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}_{B}\right)_{+} whenever σA∈ℬ​(ℋA)+\sigma_{A}\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}_{A}\right)_{+}. Let idA denote the identity map acting on a system AA. A linear map 𝒩A→B\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow B} is completely positive if the map idR⊗𝒩A→B{}_{R}\otimes\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow B} is positive for a reference system RR of arbitrary size. A linear map 𝒩A→B\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow B} is trace-preserving if Tr{𝒩A→B​(τA)}=\left\{\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow B}\left(\tau_{A}\right)\right\}=\ Tr{τA}\left\{\tau_{A}\right\} for all input operators τA∈ℬ⁡(ℋA)\tau_{A}\in\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{H}_{A}\right). If a linear map is completely positive and trace-preserving (CPTP), we say that it is a quantum channel or quantum operation. An extension of a state ρA∈𝒮⁡(ℋA)\rho_{A}\in\mathcal{S}\left(\mathcal{H}_{A}\right) is some state ΩR​A∈𝒮⁡(ℋR⊗ℋA)\Omega_{RA}\in\mathcal{S}\left(\mathcal{H}_{R}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{A}\right) such that TrR​{ΩR​A}=ρA\mathrm{Tr}_{R}\left\{\Omega_{RA}\right\}=\rho_{A}. An isometric extension UA→B​E𝒩U_{A\rightarrow BE}^{\mathcal{N}} of a channel 𝒩A→B\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow B} acting on a state ρA∈𝒮⁡(ℋA)\rho_{A}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}_{A}) is a linear map that satisfies the following:

TrE​{UA→B​E𝒩​ρA​(UA→B​E𝒩)†}=𝒩A→B​(ρA),U𝒩†​U𝒩=IA,U𝒩​U𝒩†=ΠB​E,\mathrm{Tr}_{E}\left\{U_{A\rightarrow BE}^{\mathcal{N}}\rho_{A}(U_{A\rightarrow BE}^{\mathcal{N}})^{{\dagger}}\right\}=\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow B}\left(\rho_{A}\right),\ \ \ \ \ U_{\mathcal{N}}^{\dagger}U_{\mathcal{N}}=I_{A},\ \ \ \ \ U_{\mathcal{N}}U_{\mathcal{N}}^{\dagger}=\Pi_{BE}, (3.8)

where ΠB​E\Pi_{BE} is a projection onto a subspace of the Hilbert space ℋB⊗ℋE\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{E}.

4 Fidelity of recovery

In this section, we formally define the fidelity of recovery for a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, and we prove that it possesses various properties, demonstrating that the quantity IF​(A;B|C)ρI_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho} defined in (2.1) is similar to the conditional mutual information.

Definition 1 (Fidelity of recovery)

Let ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} be a tripartite state. The fidelity of recovery for ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} with respect to system AA is defined as follows:

F​(A;B|C)ρ≡supℛC→A​CF⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛC→A​C​(ρB​C)).F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\equiv\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}}F\left(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right). (4.1)

This quantity characterizes how well one can recover the full state on systems A​B​CABC from system CC alone if system AA is lost.

Proposition 2 (Duality)

Let ϕA​B​C​D\phi_{ABCD} denote a four-party pure state. Then

F​(A;B|C)ϕ=F​(A;B|D)ϕ,F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\phi}=F\left(A;B|D\right)_{\phi}, (4.2)

which is equivalent to

IF​(A;B|C)ϕ=IF​(A;B|D)ϕ.I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\phi}=I_{F}\left(A;B|D\right)_{\phi}. (4.3)

Proof. By definition,

F​(A;B|C)ϕ=supℛC→A​C1F⁡(ϕA​B​C,ℛC→A​C1​(ϕB​C)).F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\phi}=\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{1}}F\left(\phi_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{1}\left(\phi_{BC}\right)\right). (4.4)

Let UC→A​C​Eℛ1U_{C\rightarrow ACE}^{\mathcal{R}^{1}} be an isometric extension of ℛC→A​C1\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{1}. Since ϕA​B​C​D\phi_{ABCD} is a purification of ϕA​B​C\phi_{ABC} and UC→A​C​Eℛ1​(ϕB​C​A′​D)U_{C\rightarrow ACE}^{\mathcal{R}^{1}}\left(\phi_{BCA^{\prime}D}\right) is a purification of ℛC→A​C1​(ϕB​C)\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{1}\left(\phi_{BC}\right), we can apply Uhlmann’s theorem for fidelity to conclude that

supℛC→A​C1F⁡(ϕA​B​C,ℛC→A​C1​(ϕB​C))=supUD→A′​D​EsupUC→A​C​Eℛ1F⁡(UD→A′​D​E​(ϕA​B​C​D),UC→A​C​Eℛ1​(ϕB​C​A′​D)).\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{1}}F\left(\phi_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}^{1}\left(\phi_{BC}\right)\right)=\sup_{U_{D\rightarrow A^{\prime}DE}}\sup_{U_{C\rightarrow ACE}^{\mathcal{R}^{1}}}F\left(U_{D\rightarrow A^{\prime}DE}\left(\phi_{ABCD}\right),U_{C\rightarrow ACE}^{\mathcal{R}^{1}}\left(\phi_{BCA^{\prime}D}\right)\right). (4.5)

Now consider that

F​(A;B|D)ϕ=supℛD→A​D2F⁡(ϕA​B​D,ℛD→A​D2​(ϕB​D)).F\left(A;B|D\right)_{\phi}=\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow AD}^{2}}F\left(\phi_{ABD},\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow AD}^{2}\left(\phi_{BD}\right)\right). (4.6)

Let UD→A​D​Eℛ2U_{D\rightarrow ADE}^{\mathcal{R}^{2}} be an isometric extension of ℛD→A​D2\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow AD}^{2}. Since ϕA​B​C​D\phi_{ABCD} is a purification of ϕA​B​D\phi_{ABD} and UD→A​D​Eℛ2​(ϕB​D​A′​C)U_{D\rightarrow ADE}^{\mathcal{R}^{2}}\left(\phi_{BDA^{\prime}C}\right) is a purification of ℛD→A​D2​(ϕB​D)\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow AD}^{2}\left(\phi_{BD}\right), we can apply Uhlmann’s theorem for fidelity to conclude that

supℛD→A​D2F⁡(ϕA​B​D,ℛD→A​D2​(ϕB​D))=supUC→A′​C​EsupUD→A​D​Eℛ2F⁡(UC→A′​C​E​(ϕA​B​C​D),UD→A​D​Eℛ2​(ϕB​D​A′​C)).\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow AD}^{2}}F\left(\phi_{ABD},\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow AD}^{2}\left(\phi_{BD}\right)\right)=\sup_{U_{C\rightarrow A^{\prime}CE}}\sup_{U_{D\rightarrow ADE}^{\mathcal{R}^{2}}}F\left(U_{C\rightarrow A^{\prime}CE}\left(\phi_{ABCD}\right),U_{D\rightarrow ADE}^{\mathcal{R}^{2}}\left(\phi_{BDA^{\prime}C}\right)\right). (4.7)

By inspecting the RHS of (4.5) and the RHS of (4.7), we see that the two expressions are equivalent so that the statement of the proposition holds. Figure 1 gives a graphical depiction of this proof which should help in determining which systems are “connected together” and furthermore highlights how the duality between the recovery map and the map from Uhlmann’s theorem is reflected in the duality for the fidelity of recovery.  

Remark 3

The physical interpretation of the above duality is as follows: beginning with a four-party pure state ϕA​B​C​D\phi_{ABCD}, suppose that system AA is lost. Then one can recover the state on systems A​B​CABC\ from system CC alone just as well as one can recover the state on systems A​B​DABD from system DD alone.

Proposition 4 (Monotonicity)

The fidelity of recovery is monotone under local operations on systems AA and BB, in the sense that

F​(A;B|C)ρ≤F​(A′;B′|C)τ,F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\leq F\left(A^{\prime};B^{\prime}|C\right)_{\tau}, (4.8)

where τA′​B′​C≡(𝒩A→A′⊗ℳB→B′)​(ρA​B​C)\tau_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}C}\equiv\left(\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\right)\left(\rho_{ABC}\right). The above inequality is equivalent to

IF​(A;B|C)ρ≥IF​(A′;B′|C)τ.I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\geq I_{F}\left(A^{\prime};B^{\prime}|C\right)_{\tau}. (4.9)

Proof. For any recovery map ℛC→A​C\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}, we have that

F⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛC→A​C​(ρB​C))\displaystyle F\left(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right) (4.10)
≤F⁡((𝒩A→A′⊗ℳB→B′)​(ρA​B​C),(𝒩A→A′⊗ℳB→B′)​(ℛC→A​C​(ρB​C)))\displaystyle\leq F\left(\left(\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\right)\left(\rho_{ABC}\right),\left(\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\right)\left(\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right)\right) (4.11)
=F⁡((𝒩A→A′⊗ℳB→B′)​(ρA​B​C),(𝒩A→A′∘ℛC→A​C)​(ℳB→B′​(ρB​C)))\displaystyle=F\left(\left(\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\right)\left(\rho_{ABC}\right),\left(\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}\right)\left(\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right)\right) (4.12)
≤supℛC→A′​CF⁡((𝒩A→A′⊗ℳB→B′)​(ρA​B​C),ℛC→A′​C​(ℳB→B′​(ρB​C)))\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow A^{\prime}C}}F\left(\left(\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\right)\left(\rho_{ABC}\right),\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow A^{\prime}C}\left(\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right)\right) (4.13)
=F​(A′;B′|C)(𝒩⊗ℳ)​(ρ),\displaystyle=F\left(A^{\prime};B^{\prime}|C\right)_{\left(\mathcal{N\otimes M}\right)\left(\rho\right)}, (4.14)

where the first inequality is due to monotonicity of the fidelity under quantum operations. Since the chain of inequalities holds for all ℛC→A​C\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}, it follows that

F​(A;B|C)ρ=supℛC→A​CF⁡(ρA​B​C,ℛC→A​C​(ρB​C))≤F​(A′;B′|C)(𝒩⊗ℳ)​(ρ).F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}=\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}}F\left(\rho_{ABC},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}\left(\rho_{BC}\right)\right)\leq F\left(A^{\prime};B^{\prime}|C\right)_{\left(\mathcal{N\otimes M}\right)\left(\rho\right)}. (4.15)

 

Remark 5

The only property of the fidelity used to prove the above proposition is that it is monotone under quantum operations. This suggests that we can construct a fidelity-of-recovery-like measure from any “generalized divergence” (a function that is monotone under quantum operations).

Remark 6

The physical interpretation of the above monotonicity under local operations is as follows: for a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, suppose that system AA is lost. Then it is easier to recover the state on systems A​B​CABC from CC alone if there is local noise applied to systems AA or BB or both, before system AA is lost (and thus before attempting the recovery).

Proposition 7 (Dimension bound)

The fidelity of recovery obeys the following dimension bound:

F​(A;B|C)ρ≥1|A|2,F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\geq\frac{1}{\left|A\right|^{2}}, (4.16)

which is equivalent to

IF​(A;B|C)ρ≤2​log⁡|A|.I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\leq 2\log\left|A\right|. (4.17)

Proof. Consider that the following inequality holds, simply by choosing the recovery map to be one in which we do not do anything to system CC and prepare the maximally mixed state πA≡IA/|A|\pi_{A}\equiv I_{A}/\left|A\right| on system AA:

F​(A;B|C)ρ\displaystyle F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho} ≥F⁡(ρA​B​C,πA⊗ρB​C)\displaystyle\geq F\left(\rho_{ABC},\pi_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC}\right) (4.18)
=1|A|​F​(ρA​B​C,IA⊗ρB​C)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\left|A\right|}F\left(\rho_{ABC},I_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC}\right) (4.19)
≥1|A|​[Tr⁡{ρA​B​C​IA⊗ρB​C}]2.\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\left|A\right|}\left[\operatorname{Tr}\left\{\sqrt{\rho_{ABC}}\sqrt{I_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC}}\right\}\right]^{2}. (4.20)

Taking a negative logarithm and letting ϕA​B​C​D\phi_{ABCD} be a purification of ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, we find that

IF​(A;B|C)ρ\displaystyle I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho} ≤log⁡|A|−2​log⁡Tr⁡{ρA​B​C​IA⊗ρB​C}\displaystyle\leq\log\left|A\right|-2\log\operatorname{Tr}\left\{\sqrt{\rho_{ABC}}\sqrt{I_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC}}\right\} (4.21)
=log⁡|A|−H1/2​(A|B​C)ρ\displaystyle=\log\left|A\right|-H_{1/2}\left(A|BC\right)_{\rho} (4.22)
=log⁡|A|+H3/2​(A|D)ρ\displaystyle=\log\left|A\right|+H_{3/2}\left(A|D\right)_{\rho} (4.23)
≤log⁡|A|+H3/2​(A)ρ\displaystyle\leq\log\left|A\right|+H_{3/2}\left(A\right)_{\rho} (4.24)
≤2​log⁡|A|.\displaystyle\leq 2\log\left|A\right|. (4.25)

The first equality follows by recognizing that the second term is a conditional Rényi entropy of order 1/2 [TCR09, Definition 3]. The second equality follows from a duality relation for this conditional Rényi entropy [TCR09, Lemma 6]. The second inequality is a consequence of the quantum data processing inequality for conditional Rényi entropies [TCR09, Lemma 5] (with the map taken to be a partial trace over system DD). The last inequality follows from a dimension bound which holds for any Rényi entropy.  

Proposition 8 (Weak chain rule)

Given a four-party state ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD}, the following inequality holds

IF​(A​C;B|D)ρ≥IF​(A;B|C​D)ρ.I_{F}\left(AC;B|D\right)_{\rho}\geq I_{F}\left(A;B|CD\right)_{\rho}. (4.26)

Proof. The inequality is equivalent to

F​(A​C;B|D)ρ≤F​(A;B|C​D)ρ,F\left(AC;B|D\right)_{\rho}\leq F\left(A;B|CD\right)_{\rho}, (4.27)

which follows from the fact that it is easier to recover AA from C​DCD than it is to recover both AA and CC from DD alone. Indeed, let ℛD→A​C​D\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow ACD} be any recovery map. Then

F⁡(ρA​B​C​D,ℛD→A​C​D​(ρB​D))\displaystyle F\left(\rho_{ABCD},\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow ACD}\left(\rho_{BD}\right)\right) =F⁡(ρA​B​C​D,(ℛD→A​C​D∘TrC)​(ρB​C​D))\displaystyle=F\left(\rho_{ABCD},\left(\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow ACD}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{C}\right)\left(\rho_{BCD}\right)\right) (4.28)
≤supℛC​D→A​C​DF⁡(ρA​B​C​D,(ℛC​D→A​C​D)​(ρB​C​D))\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{CD\rightarrow ACD}}F\left(\rho_{ABCD},\left(\mathcal{R}_{CD\rightarrow ACD}\right)\left(\rho_{BCD}\right)\right) (4.29)
=F​(A;B|C​D)ρ.\displaystyle=F\left(A;B|CD\right)_{\rho}. (4.30)

Since the chain of inequalities holds for any recovery map ℛD→A​C​D\mathcal{R}_{D\rightarrow ACD}, we can conclude (4.27) from the definition of F​(A​C;B|D)ρF\left(AC;B|D\right)_{\rho}.  

Proposition 9 (Conditioning on classical information)

Let ωA​B​C​X\omega_{ABCX} be a state for which system XX is classical:

ωA​B​C​X=∑xpX(x)ωA​B​Cx⊗|x⟩⟨x|X,\omega_{ABCX}=\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\omega_{ABC}^{x}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X}, (4.31)

where {|x⟩X}\left\{\left|x\right\rangle_{X}\right\} is an orthonormal basis, pX​(x)p_{X}\left(x\right) is a probability distribution, and each ωA​B​Cx\omega_{ABC}^{x} is a state. Then the following equalities hold

F​(A;B|C​X)ω\displaystyle F\left(A;B|CX\right)_{\omega} =[∑xpX​(x)​F​(A;B|C)ωx]2,\displaystyle=\left[\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sqrt{F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\omega^{x}}}\right]^{2}, (4.32)
IF​(A;B|C​X)ω\displaystyle I_{F}\left(A;B|CX\right)_{\omega} =−2​log⁡[∑xpX​(x)​exp⁡{−12​IF​(A;B|C)ωx}].\displaystyle=-2\log\left[\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\omega^{x}}\right\}\right]. (4.33)

Proof. We first prove the inequality

F​(A;B|C​X)ω≤∑xpX​(x)​F​(A;B|C)ωx.\sqrt{F\left(A;B|CX\right)_{\omega}}\leq\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sqrt{F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\omega^{x}}}. (4.34)

Let ℛC​X→C​X​A\mathcal{R}_{CX\rightarrow CXA} be any recovery map taking systems C​XCX to systems C​X​ACXA, and let ℛC→C​X​Ax\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CXA}^{x} be defined by

ℛC→C​X​Ax(σC)≡ℛC​X→C​X​A(σC⊗|x⟩⟨x|X).\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CXA}^{x}\left(\sigma_{C}\right)\equiv\mathcal{R}_{CX\rightarrow CXA}\left(\sigma_{C}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X}\right). (4.35)

Then

F(∑xpX(x)ωA​B​Cx⊗|x⟩⟨x|X,ℛC​X→C​X​A(∑xpX(x)ωB​Cx⊗|x⟩⟨x|X))\displaystyle\sqrt{F\left(\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\omega_{ABC}^{x}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X},\mathcal{R}_{CX\rightarrow CXA}\left(\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\omega_{BC}^{x}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X}\right)\right)}
=F(∑xpX(x)ωA​B​Cx⊗|x⟩⟨x|X,∑xpX(x)ℛC→C​X​Ax(ωB​Cx))\displaystyle=\sqrt{F\left(\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\omega_{ABC}^{x}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X},\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CXA}^{x}\left(\omega_{BC}^{x}\right)\right)} (4.36)
≤∑xpX​(x)​F(ωA​B​Cx⊗|x⟩⟨x|X,ℛC→C​X​Ax(ωB​Cx))\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sqrt{F\left(\omega_{ABC}^{x}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CXA}^{x}\left(\omega_{BC}^{x}\right)\right)} (4.37)
≤∑xpX​(x)​F⁡(ωA​B​Cx,ℛC→C​Ax​(ωB​Cx))\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sqrt{F\left(\omega_{ABC}^{x},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}\left(\omega_{BC}^{x}\right)\right)} (4.38)
≤∑xpX​(x)​sup{ℛC→C​Ax}F⁡(ωA​B​Cx,ℛC→C​Ax​(ωB​Cx))\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sup_{\left\{\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}\right\}}\sqrt{F\left(\omega_{ABC}^{x},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}\left(\omega_{BC}^{x}\right)\right)} (4.39)
=∑xpX​(x)​F​(A;B|C)ωx.\displaystyle=\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sqrt{F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\omega^{x}}}. (4.40)

The first inequality follows from joint concavity of the root fidelity [NC10, Theorem 9.7], the second from monotonicity of the fidelity under the discarding of system XX, and the third by taking a supremum over each of the individual recovery maps ℛC→C​Ax\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}. Since the inequality holds universally for any recovery map ℛC​X→C​X​A\mathcal{R}_{CX\rightarrow CXA}, we can conclude (4.34).

We now prove the other inequality:

F​(A;B|C​X)ω≥∑xpX​(x)​F​(A;B|C)ωx.\sqrt{F\left(A;B|CX\right)_{\omega}}\geq\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sqrt{F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\omega^{x}}}. (4.41)

For any set of recovery maps ℛC→C​Ax\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}, define ℛC​X→C​X​A\mathcal{R}_{CX\rightarrow CXA} as follows:

ℛC​X→C​X​A(τC​X)≡∑xℛC→C​Ax(⟨x|X(τC​X)|x⟩X)|x⟩⟨x|X,\mathcal{R}_{CX\rightarrow CXA}\left(\tau_{CX}\right)\equiv\sum_{x}\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}\left(\left\langle x\right|_{X}\left(\tau_{CX}\right)\left|x\right\rangle_{X}\right)\ \left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X}, (4.42)

so that it first measures the system XX in the basis {|x⟩⟨x|X}\left\{\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X}\right\}, places the outcome in the same classical register, and then acts with the particular recovery map ℛC→C​Ax\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}. Then

[∑xpX​(x)​F⁡(ωA​B​Cx,ℛC→C​Ax​(ωB​Cx))]2\displaystyle\left[\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sqrt{F\left(\omega_{ABC}^{x},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}\left(\omega_{BC}^{x}\right)\right)}\right]^{2}
=F(∑xpX(x)ωA​B​Cx⊗|x⟩⟨x|X,∑xpX(x)ℛC→C​Ax(ωB​Cx)⊗|x⟩⟨x|X)\displaystyle=F\left(\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\omega_{ABC}^{x}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X},\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}\left(\omega_{BC}^{x}\right)\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X}\right) (4.43)
=F(∑xpX(x)ωA​B​Cx⊗|x⟩⟨x|X,ℛC​X→C​X​A(∑xpX(x)ωB​Cx⊗|x⟩⟨x|X))\displaystyle=F\left(\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\omega_{ABC}^{x}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X},\mathcal{R}_{CX\rightarrow CXA}\left(\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\omega_{BC}^{x}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X}\right)\right) (4.44)
≤F​(A;B|C​X)ω.\displaystyle\leq F\left(A;B|CX\right)_{\omega}. (4.45)

Since the inequality holds for any set of individual recovery maps {ℛC→C​Ax}\left\{\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow CA}^{x}\right\}, we obtain (4.41).

Combining (4.34) with (4.41) gives (4.32).

Finally, we recover (4.33) from the equality in (4.32) and definitions.  

Applying convexity of x2x^{2} and convexity of −log-\log to Proposition 9 gives the following corollary:

Corollary 10

Let ωA​B​C​X\omega_{ABCX} be a state for which system XX is classical. Then

F​(A;B|C​X)ω\displaystyle F\left(A;B|CX\right)_{\omega} ≤∑xpX​(x)​F​(A;B|C)ωx,\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\omega^{x}}, (4.46)
IF​(A;B|C​X)ω\displaystyle I_{F}\left(A;B|CX\right)_{\omega} ≤∑xpX​(x)​IF​(A;B|C)ωx.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\omega^{x}}. (4.47)
Proposition 11 (Conditioning on a product system)

Let ρA​B​C=σA​B⊗ωC\rho_{ABC}=\sigma_{AB}\otimes\omega_{C}. Then

F​(A;B|C)ρ\displaystyle F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho} =F​(A,B)σ≡supτAF⁡(σA​B,τA⊗σB),\displaystyle=F\left(A;B\right)_{\sigma}\equiv\sup_{\tau_{A}}F\left(\sigma_{AB},\tau_{A}\otimes\sigma_{B}\right), (4.48)
IF​(A;B|C)ρ\displaystyle I_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho} =IF​(A,B)σ≡−log⁡F​(A,B)σ.\displaystyle=I_{F}\left(A;B\right)_{\sigma}\equiv-\log F\left(A;B\right)_{\sigma}. (4.49)

Proof. Consider that, for any recovery map ℛC→A​C\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}

F⁡(σA​B⊗ωC,ℛC→A​C​(σB⊗ωC))\displaystyle F\left(\sigma_{AB}\otimes\omega_{C},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}\left(\sigma_{B}\otimes\omega_{C}\right)\right) =F⁡(σA​B⊗ωC,σB⊗ℛC→A​C​(ωC))\displaystyle=F\left(\sigma_{AB}\otimes\omega_{C},\sigma_{B}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}\left(\omega_{C}\right)\right) (4.50)
≤F⁡(σA​B,σB⊗ℛC→A​(ωC))\displaystyle\leq F\left(\sigma_{AB},\sigma_{B}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow A}\left(\omega_{C}\right)\right) (4.51)
≤supτAF⁡(σA​B,σB⊗τA).\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\tau_{A}}F\left(\sigma_{AB},\sigma_{B}\otimes\tau_{A}\right). (4.52)

The first inequality follows because fidelity is monotone under partial trace over the CC system. The second inequality follows by optimizing the second argument to the fidelity over all states on the AA system. Since the inequality holds independent of the recovery map ℛC→A​C\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}, this proves that

F​(A;B|C)ρ≤F​(A,B)σ.F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}\leq F\left(A;B\right)_{\sigma}. (4.53)

To prove the other inequality F​(A,B)σ≤F​(A;B|C)ρF\left(A;B\right)_{\sigma}\leq F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}, consider for any state τA\tau_{A} that

F⁡(σA​B,σB⊗τA)\displaystyle F\left(\sigma_{AB},\sigma_{B}\otimes\tau_{A}\right) =F⁡(σA​B⊗ωC,σB⊗τA⊗ωC)\displaystyle=F\left(\sigma_{AB}\otimes\omega_{C},\sigma_{B}\otimes\tau_{A}\otimes\omega_{C}\right) (4.54)
=F⁡(σA​B⊗ωC,(idC⊗𝒫Aτ)​(σB⊗ωC))\displaystyle=F\left(\sigma_{AB}\otimes\omega_{C},\left(\text{id}_{C}\otimes\mathcal{P}_{A}^{\tau}\right)\left(\sigma_{B}\otimes\omega_{C}\right)\right) (4.55)
≤supℛC→A​CF⁡(σA​B⊗ωC,ℛC→A​C​(σB⊗ωC)).\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}}F\left(\sigma_{AB}\otimes\omega_{C},\mathcal{R}_{C\rightarrow AC}\left(\sigma_{B}\otimes\omega_{C}\right)\right). (4.56)

The first equality follows because fidelity is multiplicative under tensor-product states. The second equality follows by taking (idC⊗𝒫Aτ)\left(\text{id}_{C}\otimes\mathcal{P}_{A}^{\tau}\right) to be the recovery map that does nothing to system CC and prepares τA\tau_{A} on system AA. The inequality follows by optimizing over all recovery maps. Since the inequality is independent of the prepared state, we obtain the other inequality

F​(A,B)σ≤F​(A;B|C)ρ.F\left(A;B\right)_{\sigma}\leq F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}. (4.57)

The equality IF​(A;B|C)ρ=IF​(A,B)σI_{F}\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}=I_{F}\left(A;B\right)_{\sigma} follows by applying a negative logarithm to F​(A;B|C)ρ=F​(A,B)σF\left(A;B|C\right)_{\rho}=F\left(A;B\right)_{\sigma}. We note in passing that the quantity on the RHS in (4.49) is closely related to the sandwiched Rényi mutual information of order 1/2 [MLDS+13, WWY14, Bei13, GW13].  

The following proposition gives a simple proof of the main result of [FR14] when the tripartite state of interest is pure:

Proposition 12 (Approximate quantum Markov chain)

The conditional mutual information I​(A;B|C)ψI\left(A;B|C\right)_{\psi} of a pure tripartite state ψA​B​C\psi_{ABC} has the following lower bound:

I​(A;B|C)ψ≥−log⁡F​(A;B|C)ψ.I\left(A;B|C\right)_{\psi}\geq-\log F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\psi}. (4.58)

Proof. Let φD\varphi_{D} be a pure state on an auxiliary system DD, so that |ψ⟩A​B​C⊗|φ⟩D\left|\psi\right\rangle_{ABC}\otimes\left|\varphi\right\rangle_{D} is a purification of |ψ⟩A​B​C\left|\psi\right\rangle_{ABC}. Consider the following chain of inequalities:

I​(A;B|C)ψ\displaystyle I\left(A;B|C\right)_{\psi} =I​(A;B|D)ψ⊗φ\displaystyle=I\left(A;B|D\right)_{\psi\otimes\varphi} (4.59)
=I​(A,B)ψ\displaystyle=I\left(A;B\right)_{\psi} (4.60)
≥−log⁡F⁡(ψA​B,ψA⊗ψB)\displaystyle\geq-\log F\left(\psi_{AB},\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}\right) (4.61)
≥−log⁡F​(A,B)ψ\displaystyle\geq-\log F\left(A;B\right)_{\psi} (4.62)
=−log⁡F​(A;B|D)ψ⊗φ\displaystyle=-\log F\left(A;B|D\right)_{\psi\otimes\varphi} (4.63)
=−log⁡F​(A;B|C)ψ.\displaystyle=-\log F\left(A;B|C\right)_{\psi}. (4.64)

The first equality follows from duality of conditional mutual information. The second follows because system DD is product with systems AA and BB. The first inequality follows from monotonicity of the sandwiched Rényi relative entropies [MLDS+13, Theorem 7]:

D~α(ρ∥σ)≤D~β(ρ∥σ),\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}\left(\rho\|\sigma\right)\leq\widetilde{D}_{\beta}\left(\rho\|\sigma\right), (4.65)

for states ρ\rho and σ\sigma and Rényi parameters α\alpha and β\beta such that 0≤α≤β0\leq\alpha\leq\beta. We apply this with the choices α=1/2\alpha=1/2, β=1\beta=1, ρ=ψA​B\rho=\psi_{AB}, and σ=ψA⊗ψB\sigma=\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}. The second inequality follows by optimizing over states on system AA and applying the definition in (4.49). The second-to-last equality follows from Proposition 11 and the last from Proposition 2.  

5 Geometric squashed entanglement

In this section, we formally define the geometric squashed entanglement of a bipartite state ρA​B\rho_{AB}, and we prove that it obeys the properties claimed in Section 2.

Definition 13 (Geometric squashed entanglement)

The geometric squashed entanglement of a bipartite state ρA​B\rho_{AB} is defined as follows:

EFsq​(A,B)ρ≡−12​log⁡Fsq​(A,B)ρ,E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\equiv-\frac{1}{2}\log F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}, (5.1)

where

Fsq​(A,B)ρ\displaystyle F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho} ≡supωA​B​E{F​(A;B|E)ρ:ρA​B=TrE⁡{ωA​B​E}}\displaystyle\equiv\sup_{\omega_{ABE}}\left\{F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\rho}:\rho_{AB}=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}\left\{\omega_{ABE}\right\}\right\} (5.2)
=supωA​B​EsupℛE→A​E{F⁡(ωA​B​E,ℛE→A​E​(ωB​E)):ρA​B=TrE⁡{ωA​B​E}}.\displaystyle=\sup_{\omega_{ABE}}\sup_{\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE}}\left\{F\left(\omega_{ABE},\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE}\left(\omega_{BE}\right)\right):\rho_{AB}=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}\left\{\omega_{ABE}\right\}\right\}. (5.3)

The geometric squashed entanglement can equivalently be written in terms of an optimization over “squashing channels” acting on a purifying system of the original state (cf. [CW04, Eq. (3)]):

Proposition 14

Let ρA​B\rho_{AB} be a bipartite state and let |ψ⟩A​B​E′\left|\psi\right\rangle_{ABE^{\prime}} be a fixed purification of it. Then

Fsq​(A,B)ρ=sup𝒮E′→EF​(A;B|E)𝒮⁡(ψ).F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}=\sup_{\mathcal{S}_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}}F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\mathcal{S}\left(\psi\right)}. (5.4)

Proof. We first prove the inequality Fsq​(A,B)ρ≥sup𝒮E′→EF​(A;B|E)𝒮⁡(ψ)F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\geq\sup_{\mathcal{S}_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}}F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\mathcal{S}\left(\psi\right)}. Indeed, for a given squashing channel 𝒮E′→E\mathcal{S}_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E} and purification ψA​B​E′\psi_{ABE^{\prime}}, the state 𝒮E′→E​(ψA​B​E′)\mathcal{S}_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}\left(\psi_{ABE^{\prime}}\right) is an extension of ρA​B\rho_{AB}. So it follows by definition that

F​(A;B|E)𝒮⁡(ψ)≤Fsq​(A,B)ρ.F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\mathcal{S}\left(\psi\right)}\leq F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}. (5.5)

Since the choice of squashing channel was arbitrary, the first inequality follows.

We now prove the other inequality

Fsq​(A,B)ρ≤sup𝒮E′→EF​(A;B|E)𝒮⁡(ψ).F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\leq\sup_{\mathcal{S}_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}}F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\mathcal{S}\left(\psi\right)}. (5.6)

Let ωA​B​E\omega_{ABE} be an extension of ρA​B\rho_{AB}. Let φA​B​E​E1\varphi_{ABEE_{1}} be a purification of ωA​B​E\omega_{ABE}, which is in turn also a purification of ρA​B\rho_{AB}. Since all purifications are related by isometries acting on the purifying system, we know that there exists an isometry UE′→E​E1ωU_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow EE_{1}}^{\omega} (depending on ω\omega) such that

|φ⟩A​B​E​E1=UE′→E​E1ω|ψ⟩A​B​E′.\left|\varphi\right\rangle_{ABEE_{1}}=U_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow EE_{1}}^{\omega}\left|\psi\right\rangle_{ABE^{\prime}}. (5.7)

Furthermore, we know that

ωA​B​E\displaystyle\omega_{ABE} =TrE1⁡{UE′→E​E1ω​ψA​B​E′​(UE′→E​E1ω)†}\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}_{E_{1}}\left\{U_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow EE_{1}}^{\omega}\psi_{ABE^{\prime}}\left(U_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow EE_{1}}^{\omega}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\} (5.8)
≡𝒮E′→Eω​(ψA​B​E′),\displaystyle\equiv\mathcal{S}_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}^{\omega}\left(\psi_{ABE^{\prime}}\right), (5.9)

where we define the squashing channel 𝒮E′→Eω\mathcal{S}_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}^{\omega} from the isometry UE′→E​E1ωU_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow EE_{1}}^{\omega}. So this implies that

F​(A;B|E)ω=F​(A;B|E)𝒮ω​(ψ)≤sup𝒮E′→EF​(A;B|E)𝒮⁡(ψ).F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\omega}=F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\mathcal{S}^{\omega}\left(\psi\right)}\leq\sup_{\mathcal{S}_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}}F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\mathcal{S}\left(\psi\right)}. (5.10)

Since the inequality above holds for all extensions, the inequality in (5.6) follows.  

The following statement is a direct consequence of Proposition 4:

Corollary 15

The geometric squashed entanglement is monotone under local operations on both systems AA and BB:

EFsq​(A,B)ρ≥EFsq​(A′,B′)τ,E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\geq E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A^{\prime};B^{\prime}\right)_{\tau}, (5.11)

where τA′​B′≡(𝒩A→A′⊗ℳB→B′)​(ρA​B)\tau_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}\equiv\left(\mathcal{N}_{A\rightarrow A^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{B\rightarrow B^{\prime}}\right)\left(\rho_{AB}\right). This is equivalent to

Fsq​(A,B)ρ≤Fsq​(A′,B′)τ.F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\leq F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A^{\prime};B^{\prime}\right)_{\tau}. (5.12)
Proposition 16

The geometric squashed entanglement is invariant under classical communication, in the sense that

EFsq​(A​XA,B)ρ=EFsq​(A​XA,B​XB)ρ=EFsq​(A,B​XB)ρ,E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};B\right)_{\rho}=E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};BX_{B}\right)_{\rho}=E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;BX_{B}\right)_{\rho}, (5.13)

for a state ρXA​XB​A​B\rho_{X_{A}X_{B}AB} defined as

ρXA​XB​A​B≡∑xpX(x)|x⟩⟨x|XA⊗|x⟩⟨x|XB⊗ρA​Bx.\rho_{X_{A}X_{B}AB}\equiv\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X_{A}}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X_{B}}\otimes\rho_{AB}^{x}. (5.14)

This is equivalent to

Fsq​(A​XA,B)ρ=Fsq​(A​XA,B​XB)ρ=Fsq​(A,B​XB)ρ.F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};B\right)_{\rho}=F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};BX_{B}\right)_{\rho}=F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;BX_{B}\right)_{\rho}. (5.15)

Proof. From monotonicity under local operations, we have that

Fsq​(A​XA,B​XB)ρ\displaystyle F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};BX_{B}\right)_{\rho} ≤Fsq​(A​XA,B)ρ,\displaystyle\leq F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};B\right)_{\rho}, (5.16)
Fsq​(A​XA,B​XB)ρ\displaystyle F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};BX_{B}\right)_{\rho} ≤Fsq​(A,B​XB)ρ.\displaystyle\leq F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;BX_{B}\right)_{\rho}. (5.17)

So we need to show the opposite inequalities. Let ρXA​A​B​E\rho_{X_{A}ABE} be any extension of ρXA​A​B\rho_{X_{A}AB}. Let |φρ⟩XA​XR​A​B​E​R\left|\varphi^{\rho}\right\rangle_{X_{A}X_{R}ABER} be a purification of ρXA​A​B​E\rho_{X_{A}ABE}, taken as

|φρ⟩XA​XR​A​B​E​R≡∑xpX​(x)|x⟩XA|x⟩XR|φρx⟩A​B​E​R,\left|\varphi^{\rho}\right\rangle_{X_{A}X_{R}ABER}\equiv\sum_{x}\sqrt{p_{X}\left(x\right)}\left|x\right\rangle_{X_{A}}\left|x\right\rangle_{X_{R}}\left|\varphi^{\rho_{x}}\right\rangle_{ABER}, (5.18)

where each |φρx⟩A​B​E​R\left|\varphi^{\rho_{x}}\right\rangle_{ABER} purifies ρA​B​Ex\rho_{ABE}^{x}. Let φ¯XA​XB​XR​A​B​E​Rρ\overline{\varphi}_{X_{A}X_{B}X_{R}ABER}^{\rho} be defined as

φ¯XA​XB​XR​A​B​E​Rρ≡∑xpX(x)|x⟩⟨x|XA⊗|x⟩⟨x|XB⊗|x⟩⟨x|XR⊗φA​B​E​Rρx.\overline{\varphi}_{X_{A}X_{B}X_{R}ABER}^{\rho}\equiv\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X_{A}}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X_{B}}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X_{R}}\otimes\varphi_{ABER}^{\rho_{x}}. (5.19)

Let θXA​XB​XR​A​B​E​R​F\theta_{X_{A}X_{B}X_{R}ABERF} be a purification of φ¯XA​XB​XR​A​B​E​Rρ\overline{\varphi}_{X_{A}X_{B}X_{R}ABER}^{\rho}. We then have that

F​(A​XA;B|E)ρ\displaystyle F\left(AX_{A};B|E\right)_{\rho} =F​(A​XA;B|XR​R)φρ\displaystyle=F\left(AX_{A};B|X_{R}R\right)_{\varphi^{\rho}} (5.20)
≤F​(A​XA;B|XR​R)φ¯ρ,\displaystyle\leq F\left(AX_{A};B|X_{R}R\right)_{\overline{\varphi}^{\rho}}, (5.21)

where the inequality follows from processing system XAX_{A} with a completely dephasing map. Let ℛXR​R→XR​R​A​XA\mathcal{R}_{X_{R}R\rightarrow X_{R}RAX_{A}} be any CPTP map. When such a map acts on a classical system XRX_{R}, we can think of it as a collection of maps, conditioned on the value in the register XRX_{R}, i.e., {ℛR→XR​R​A​XAx}\left\{\mathcal{R}_{R\rightarrow X_{R}RAX_{A}}^{x}\right\}. So we then have that

F⁡(φ¯A​XA​B​XR​Rρ,ℛXR​R→XR​R​A​XA​(φ¯B​XR​Rρ))\displaystyle F\left(\overline{\varphi}_{AX_{A}BX_{R}R}^{\rho},\mathcal{R}_{X_{R}R\rightarrow X_{R}RAX_{A}}\left(\overline{\varphi}_{BX_{R}R}^{\rho}\right)\right)
=[∑xpX​(x)​F⁡(φA​B​E​Rρx,ℛR→XR​R​A​XAx​(φB​Rρx))]2\displaystyle=\left[\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sqrt{F\left(\varphi_{ABER}^{\rho_{x}},\mathcal{R}_{R\rightarrow X_{R}RAX_{A}}^{x}\left(\varphi_{BR}^{\rho_{x}}\right)\right)}\right]^{2} (5.22)
=[∑xpX​(x)​F(φA​B​E​Rρx⊗|x⟩⟨x|XB,ℛR→XR​R​A​XAx(φB​Rρx)⊗|x⟩⟨x|XB)]2\displaystyle=\left[\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\sqrt{F\left(\varphi_{ABER}^{\rho_{x}}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X_{B}},\mathcal{R}_{R\rightarrow X_{R}RAX_{A}}^{x}\left(\varphi_{BR}^{\rho_{x}}\right)\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X_{B}}\right)}\right]^{2} (5.23)
=F⁡(φ¯A​XA​B​XB​XR​Rρ,ℛXR​R→XR​R​A​XA​(φ¯B​XB​XR​Rρ))\displaystyle=F\left(\overline{\varphi}_{AX_{A}BX_{B}X_{R}R}^{\rho},\mathcal{R}_{X_{R}R\rightarrow X_{R}RAX_{A}}\left(\overline{\varphi}_{BX_{B}X_{R}R}^{\rho}\right)\right) (5.24)
≤F​(A​XA;B​XB|R​XR)φ¯ρ\displaystyle\leq F\left(AX_{A};BX_{B}|RX_{R}\right)_{\overline{\varphi}^{\rho}} (5.25)
≤Fsq​(A​XA,B​XB)ρ\displaystyle\leq F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};BX_{B}\right)_{\rho} (5.26)

The first equality is a property of the quantum fidelity. The second equality results because the fidelity is multiplicative under tensor-product states. The third equality follows for the same reason that the first one does. The first inequality follows from Definition 1 and the last inequality follows from Definition 13. Since the chain of inequalities above holds for all extensions of ρA​XA​B\rho_{AX_{A}B}, we can conclude the following inequality:

Fsq​(A​XA,B)ρ≤Fsq​(A​XA,B​XB)ρ.F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};B\right)_{\rho}\leq F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};BX_{B}\right)_{\rho}. (5.27)

By the same line of reasoning, we can conclude

Fsq​(A,B​XB)ρ≤Fsq​(A​XA,B​XB)ρ,F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;BX_{B}\right)_{\rho}\leq F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AX_{A};BX_{B}\right)_{\rho}, (5.28)

and thus the statement of the proposition.  

The following theorem is a direct consequence of Corollary 15 and Proposition 16:

Theorem 17 (LOCC monotone)

The geometric squashed entanglement is an LOCC monotone.

Theorem 18 (Convexity)

The geometric squashed entanglement is convex, i.e.,

∑xpX​(x)​EFsq​(A,B)ρx≥EFsq​(A,B)ρ¯,\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho^{x}}\geq E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\overline{\rho}}, (5.29)

where

ρ¯A​B≡∑xpX​(x)​ρA​Bx.\overline{\rho}_{AB}\equiv\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\rho_{AB}^{x}. (5.30)

Proof. Let ρA​B​Ex\rho_{ABE}^{x} be an extension of each ρA​Bx\rho_{AB}^{x}, so that

ωX​A​B​E≡∑xpX(x)|x⟩⟨x|X⊗ρA​B​Ex\omega_{XABE}\equiv\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{X}\otimes\rho_{ABE}^{x} (5.31)

is some extension of ρ¯A​B\overline{\rho}_{AB}. Then the definition of EFsq​(A,B)ρ¯E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\overline{\rho}} and Corollary 10 give that

2​EFsq​(A,B)ρ¯≤IF​(A;B|E​X)ω≤∑xpX​(x)​IF​(A;B|E)ρx.2E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\overline{\rho}}\leq I_{F}\left(A;B|EX\right)_{\omega}\leq\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)I_{F}\left(A;B|E\right)_{\rho^{x}}.

Since the inequality holds independent of each particular extension of ρA​Bx\rho_{AB}^{x}, we can conclude (5.29).  

Theorems 17 and 18 immediately lead to the following corollary:

Corollary 19 (Entanglement monotone)

The geometric squashed entanglement is an entanglement monotone.

Theorem 20 (Faithfulness)

The geometric squashed entanglement is faithful, in the sense that

EFsq(A;B)ρ=0if and only if ρA​B is separable.E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}=0~\text{if and only if }\rho_{AB}\text{ is separable.} (5.32)

This is equivalent to

Fsq​(A,B)ρ=1​if and only if ​ρA​B​ is separable.F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}=1~\text{if and only if }\rho_{AB}\text{ is separable.} (5.33)

Furthermore, we have the following bound holding for states with small geometric squashed entanglement:

EFsq​(A,B)ρ≥1512​|A|4​‖ρA​B−SEP⁡(A:B)‖14.E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\geq\frac{1}{512\left|A\right|^{4}}\left\|\rho_{AB}-\operatorname{SEP}(A:B)\right\|_{1}^{4}. (5.34)

Proof. We first prove the if-part of the theorem. So, given by assumption that ρA​B\rho_{AB} is separable, it has a decomposition of the following form:

ρA​B=∑xpX(x)|ψx⟩⟨ψx|A⊗|ϕx⟩⟨ϕx|B.\rho_{AB}=\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\left|\psi_{x}\right\rangle\left\langle\psi_{x}\right|_{A}\otimes\left|\phi_{x}\right\rangle\left\langle\phi_{x}\right|_{B}. (5.35)

Then an extension of the state is of the form

ρA​B​E=∑xpX(x)|ψx⟩⟨ψx|A⊗|ϕx⟩⟨ϕx|B⊗|x⟩⟨x|E.\rho_{ABE}=\sum_{x}p_{X}\left(x\right)\left|\psi_{x}\right\rangle\left\langle\psi_{x}\right|_{A}\otimes\left|\phi_{x}\right\rangle\left\langle\phi_{x}\right|_{B}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{E}. (5.36)

Clearly, if the system AA becomes lost, someone who possesses system EE could measure it and prepare the state |ψx⟩A\left|\psi_{x}\right\rangle_{A} conditioned on the measurement outcome. That is, the recover map ℛE→A​E\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE} is as follows:

ℛE→A​E(σE)=∑x⟨x|σE|x⟩|ψx⟩⟨ψx|A⊗|x⟩⟨x|E.\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE}\left(\sigma_{E}\right)=\sum_{x}\left\langle x\right|\sigma_{E}\left|x\right\rangle\ \left|\psi_{x}\right\rangle\left\langle\psi_{x}\right|_{A}\otimes\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|_{E}. (5.37)

So this implies that

F⁡(ρA​B​E,ℛE→A​E​(ρB​E))=1,F\left(\rho_{ABE},\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE}\left(\rho_{BE}\right)\right)=1, (5.38)

and thus Fsq​(A,B)ρ=1F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}=1.

The only-if-part of the theorem is a direct consequence of the reasoning in [WL12]. We repeat the argument from [WL12] here for the convenience of the reader. The reasoning from [WL12] establishes that the trace distance between ρA​B\rho_{AB} and the set SEP(A:B)(A:B) of separable states on systems AA and BB is bounded from above by a function of −1/2logFsq(A;B)ρ-1/2\log F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho} and |A|\left|A\right|. This will then allow us to conclude the only-if-part of the theorem.

Let

ε≡−1/2logFsq(A;B)ρ\varepsilon\equiv-1/2\log F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho} (5.39)

for some bipartite state ρA​B\rho_{AB} and let

εω,ℛ≡−1/2logF(ωA​B​E,ℛE→A​E(ωB​E)),\varepsilon_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}\equiv-1/2\log F(\omega_{ABE},\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE}\left(\omega_{BE}\right)), (5.40)

for some extension ωA​B​E\omega_{ABE} and a recovery map ℛE→A​E\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE}. By definition, we have that

ε=infω,ℛE→A​Eεω,ℛ.\varepsilon=\inf_{\omega,\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE}}\varepsilon_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}. (5.41)

Then consider that

εω,ℛ≥18​‖ωA​B​E−ℛE→A​E​(ωB​E)‖12,\varepsilon_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}\geq\frac{1}{8}\left\|\omega_{ABE}-\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE}\left(\omega_{BE}\right)\right\|_{1}^{2}, (5.42)

where the inequality follows from a well known relation between the fidelity and trace distance [FvdG98]. Therefore, by defining δω,ℛ=8​εω,ℛ\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}=\sqrt{8\varepsilon_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}} we have that

δω,ℛ\displaystyle\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}} ≥‖ωA​B​E−ℛE→A​E​(ωB​E)‖1\displaystyle\geq\left\|\omega_{ABE}-\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AE}\left(\omega_{BE}\right)\right\|_{1} (5.43)
=‖ωA​B​E−(ℛE→A2​E∘TrA1)​(ωA1​B​E)‖1,\displaystyle=\left\|\omega_{ABE}-\left(\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{2}E}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{1}}\right)\left(\omega_{A_{1}BE}\right)\right\|_{1}, (5.44)

where the systems A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} are defined to be isomorphic to system AA. Now consider applying the same recovery map again. We then have that

δω,ℛ≥‖(ℛE→A3​E∘TrA2)(ωA2​B​E)−○i=23(ℛE→Ai​E∘TrAi−1)(ωA1​B​E)‖1,\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}\geq\left\|\left(\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{3}E}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{2}}\right)\left(\omega_{A_{2}BE}\right)-\bigcirc_{i=2}^{3}\left(\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{i}E}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{i-1}}\right)\left(\omega_{A_{1}BE}\right)\right\|_{1}, (5.45)

which follows from the inequality above and monotonicity of the trace distance under the quantum operation ℛE→A3​E∘\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{3}E}\circTrA2{}_{A_{2}}. Combining via the triangle inequality, we find for k≥2k\geq 2 that

‖ωA​B​E−○i=23(ℛE→Ai​E∘TrAi−1)(ωA1​B​E)‖1\displaystyle\left\|\omega_{ABE}-\bigcirc_{i=2}^{3}\left(\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{i}E}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{i-1}}\right)\left(\omega_{A_{1}BE}\right)\right\|_{1} ≤2​δω,ℛ\displaystyle\leq 2\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}} (5.46)
≤k​δω,ℛ.\displaystyle\leq k\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}. (5.47)

We can iterate this reasoning in the following way: For j∈{4,…,k}j\in\left\{4,\ldots,k\right\} (assuming now k≥4k\geq 4), apply the maps ℛE→Aj​E∘\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{j}E}\circTrAj−1{}_{A_{j-1}} along with monotonicity of trace distance to establish the following inequalities:

‖[○i=3j(ℛE→Ai​E∘TrAi−1)(ωA2​B​E)]−[○i=2j(ℛE→Ai​E∘TrAi−1)(ωA1​B​E)]‖1≤δω,ℛ\left\|\left[\bigcirc_{i=3}^{j}\left(\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{i}E}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{i-1}}\right)\left(\omega_{A_{2}BE}\right)\right]-\left[\bigcirc_{i=2}^{j}\left(\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{i}E}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{i-1}}\right)\left(\omega_{A_{1}BE}\right)\right]\right\|_{1}\leq\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}} (5.48)

Apply the triangle inequality to all of these to establish the following inequalities for j∈{1,…,k}j\in\left\{1,\ldots,k\right\}:

‖ωA​B​E−○i=2j(ℛE→Ai​E∘TrAi−1)(ωA1​B​E)‖1≤kδω,ℛ,\left\|\omega_{ABE}-\bigcirc_{i=2}^{j}\left(\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{i}E}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{i-1}}\right)\left(\omega_{A_{1}BE}\right)\right\|_{1}\leq k\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}, (5.49)

with the interpretation for j=1j=1 that there is no map applied. From monotonicity of trace distance under quantum operations, we can then conclude the following inequalities for j∈{1,…,k}j\in\left\{1,\ldots,k\right\}:

‖ρA​B−TrE{○i=2j(ℛE→Ai​E∘TrAi−1)(ωA1​B​E)}‖1≤kδω,ℛ.\left\|\rho_{AB}-\operatorname{Tr}_{E}\left\{\bigcirc_{i=2}^{j}\left(\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{i}E}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{i-1}}\right)\left(\omega_{A_{1}BE}\right)\right\}\right\|_{1}\leq k\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}. (5.50)

Let γA1A2⋯AkBE\gamma_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}BE} denote the following state:

γA1A2⋯AkBE≡ℛE→Ak​E(⋯(ℛE→A2​E(ωA1​B​E))).\gamma_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}BE}\equiv\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{k}E}\left(\cdots\left(\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow A_{2}E}\left(\omega_{A_{1}BE}\right)\right)\right). (5.51)

(See Figure 2 for a graphical depiction of this state.)

Then the inequalities in (5.50) are equivalent to the following inequalities for j∈{1​…,k}j\in\left\{1\ldots,k\right\}:

‖ρA​B−γAj​B‖1≤k​δω,ℛ,\left\|\rho_{AB}-\gamma_{A_{j}B}\right\|_{1}\leq k\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}, (5.52)

which are in turn equivalent to the following ones for any permutation π∈Sk\pi\in S_{k}:

‖ρA​B−TrA2⋯Ak{WA1A2⋯AkπγA1A2⋯AkB(WA1A2⋯Akπ)†}‖1≤kδω,ℛ,\left\|\rho_{AB}-\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}\left\{W_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}^{\pi}\gamma_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}B}\left(W_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}^{\pi}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\}\right\|_{1}\leq k\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}, (5.53)

with WA1A2⋯AkπW_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}^{\pi} a unitary representation of the permutation π\pi. We can then define γ¯A1⋯AkB\overline{\gamma}_{A_{1}\cdots A_{k}B} as a symmetrized version of γA1⋯AkB\gamma_{A_{1}\cdots A_{k}B}:

γ¯A1⋯AkB≡1k!∑π∈SkWA1A2⋯AkπγA1⋯AkB(WA1A2⋯Akπ)†.\overline{\gamma}_{A_{1}\cdots A_{k}B}\equiv\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_{k}}W_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}^{\pi}\gamma_{A_{1}\cdots A_{k}B}\left(W_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}^{\pi}\right)^{{\dagger}}. (5.54)

The inequalities in (5.53) allow us to conclude that

k​δω,ℛ\displaystyle k\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}} ≥1k!∑π∈Sk‖ρA​B−TrA2⋯Ak{WA1A2⋯AkπγA1A2⋯AkB(WA1A2⋯Akπ)†}‖1\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_{k}}\left\|\rho_{AB}-\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}\left\{W_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}^{\pi}\gamma_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}B}\left(W_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}^{\pi}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\}\right\|_{1} (5.55)
≥‖ρA​B−TrA2⋯Ak{1k!∑π∈SkWA1A2⋯AkπγA1A2⋯AkB(WA1A2⋯Akπ)†}‖1\displaystyle\geq\left\|\rho_{AB}-\operatorname{Tr}_{A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}\left\{\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\pi\in S_{k}}W_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}^{\pi}\gamma_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}B}\left(W_{A_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{k}}^{\pi}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\}\right\|_{1} (5.56)
=‖ρA​B−γ¯A1​B‖1,\displaystyle=\left\|\rho_{AB}-\overline{\gamma}_{A_{1}B}\right\|_{1}, (5.57)

where the second inequality is a consequence of the convexity of trace distance. So what the reasoning in [WL12] accomplishes is to construct a kk-extendible state γ¯A1​B\overline{\gamma}_{A_{1}B} that is k​δω,ℛk\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}-close to ρA​B\rho_{AB} in trace distance.

Following [WL12], we now recall a particular quantum de Finetti result in [CKMR07, Theorem II.7’]. Consider a state ωA1⋯AkB\omega_{A_{1}\cdots A_{k}B} which is permutation invariant with respect to systems A1⋯AkA_{1}\cdots A_{k}. Let ωA1⋯AnB\omega_{A_{1}\cdots A_{n}B} denote the reduced state on nn of the kk AA systems where n≤kn\leq k. Then, for large kk, ωA1⋯AnB\omega_{A_{1}\cdots A_{n}B} is close in trace distance to a convex combination of product states of the form ∫σA⊗n⊗τ​(σ)B​𝑑μ​(σ)\int\sigma_{A}^{\otimes n}\otimes\tau\left(\sigma\right)_{B}\ d\mu(\sigma), where μ\mu is a probability measure on the set of mixed states on a single AA system and {τ⁡(σ)}σ\left\{\tau\left(\sigma\right)\right\}_{\sigma} is a family of states parametrized by σ\sigma, with the approximation given by

2​|A|2​nk≥‖ωA1⋯AnB−∫σA⊗n⊗τ(σ)Bdμ(σ)‖1.\frac{2\left|A\right|^{2}n}{k}\geq\left\|\omega_{A_{1}\cdots A_{n}B}-\int\sigma_{A}^{\otimes n}\otimes\tau\left(\sigma\right)_{B}\ d\mu(\sigma)\right\|_{1}. (5.58)

Applying this theorem in our context (choosing n=1n=1) leads to the following conclusion:

2​|A|2k\displaystyle\frac{2\left|A\right|^{2}}{k} ≥‖γ¯A1​B−∫σA1⊗τ​(σ)B​𝑑μ​(σ)‖1\displaystyle\geq\left\|\overline{\gamma}_{A_{1}B}-\int\sigma_{A_{1}}\otimes\tau\left(\sigma\right)_{B}\ d\mu(\sigma)\right\|_{1} (5.59)
≥‖γ¯A1​B−SEP​(A1:B)‖1,\displaystyle\geq\left\|\overline{\gamma}_{A_{1}B}-\text{SEP}(A_{1}:B)\right\|_{1}, (5.60)

because the state ∫σA1⊗τ​(σ)B​𝑑μ​(σ)\int\sigma_{A_{1}}\otimes\tau\left(\sigma\right)_{B}\ d\mu(\sigma) is a particular separable state.

We can now combine (5.57) and (5.60) with the triangle inequality to conclude the following bound

‖ρA​B−SEP​(A:B)‖1≤2​|A|2k+k​δω,ℛ.\left\|\rho_{AB}-\text{SEP}(A:B)\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{2|A|^{2}}{k}+k\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}. (5.61)

By choosing kk to diverge slower than δω,ℛ−1\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}^{-1}, say as k=|A|​2/δω,ℛk=|A|\sqrt{2/\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}}, we obtain the following bound:

‖ρA​B−SEP​(A:B)‖1\displaystyle\left\|\rho_{AB}-\text{SEP}(A:B)\right\|_{1} ≤|A|​8​δω,ℛ\displaystyle\leq\left|A\right|\sqrt{8\delta_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}} (5.62)
=(512)1/4​|A|​εω,ℛ1/4.\displaystyle=\left(512\right)^{1/4}\left|A\right|\varepsilon_{\omega,\mathcal{R}}^{1/4}. (5.63)

Since the above bound holds for all extensions and recovery maps, we can obtain the tightest bound by taking an infimum over all of them. By substituting with (5.39) and (5.40), we find that

‖ρA​B−SEP(A:B)‖1≤(512)1/4|A|(−1/2logFsq(A;B)ρ)1/4,\left\|\rho_{AB}-\text{SEP}(A:B)\right\|_{1}\leq\left(512\right)^{1/4}\left|A\right|\left(-1/2\log F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\right)^{1/4}, (5.64)

or equivalently

EFsq(A;B)ρ=−1/2logFsq(A;B)ρ≥1512​|A|4‖ρA​B−SEP(A:B)‖14.E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}=-1/2\log F^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\rho}\geq\frac{1}{512\left|A\right|^{4}}\left\|\rho_{AB}-\text{SEP}(A:B)\right\|_{1}^{4}. (5.65)

This proves the converse part of the faithfulness of the geometric squashed entanglement.  

Proposition 21 (Reduction to geometric measure)

Let ϕA​B\phi_{AB} be a bipartite pure state. Then

EFsq(A;B)ϕ=−12logsup|φ⟩A⟨ϕ|A​B(φA⊗ϕB)|ϕ⟩A​BE_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\phi}=-\frac{1}{2}\log\sup_{\left|\varphi\right\rangle_{A}}\left\langle\phi\right|_{AB}\left(\varphi_{A}\otimes\phi_{B}\right)\left|\phi\right\rangle_{AB} (5.66)

Proof. Any extension of a pure bipartite state is of the form ϕA​B⊗ωE\phi_{AB}\otimes\omega_{E}. Applying Proposition 11, we find that

F​(A;B|E)ϕ⊗ω\displaystyle F\left(A;B|E\right)_{\phi\otimes\omega} =F​(A,B)ϕ\displaystyle=F\left(A;B\right)_{\phi} (5.67)
=supσAF⁡(ϕA​B,ϕB⊗σA)\displaystyle=\sup_{\sigma_{A}}F\left(\phi_{AB},\phi_{B}\otimes\sigma_{A}\right) (5.68)
=sup|φ⟩A⟨ϕ|A​B(φA⊗ϕB)|ϕ⟩A​B.\displaystyle=\sup_{\left|\varphi\right\rangle_{A}}\left\langle\phi\right|_{AB}\left(\varphi_{A}\otimes\phi_{B}\right)\left|\phi\right\rangle_{AB}. (5.69)

The last equality follows due to a convexity argument applied to

F(ϕA​B,ϕB⊗σA)=⟨ϕ|A​BϕB⊗σA|ϕ⟩A​B.F\left(\phi_{AB},\phi_{B}\otimes\sigma_{A}\right)=\left\langle\phi\right|_{AB}\phi_{B}\otimes\sigma_{A}\left|\phi\right\rangle_{AB}. (5.70)

Since the equality holds independent of any particular extension of ϕA​B\phi_{AB}, we obtain the statement of the proposition upon applying a negative logarithm and dividing by two.  

Proposition 22 (Normalization)

For a maximally entangled state ΦA​B\Phi_{AB} of Schmidt rank dd,

EFsq​(A,B)Φ=log⁡d.E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(A;B\right)_{\Phi}=\log d. (5.71)

Proof. For any pure-state vector |φ⟩A\left|\varphi\right\rangle_{A}, it follows from the so-called “transpose trick” for the maximally entangled state that

⟨Φ|A​B(|φ⟩⟨φ|A⊗ΦB)|Φ⟩A​B\displaystyle\left\langle\Phi\right|_{AB}\left(\left|\varphi\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi\right|_{A}\otimes\Phi_{B}\right)\left|\Phi\right\rangle_{AB} =1d⟨φ∗|BΦB|φ∗⟩B\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\left\langle\varphi^{\ast}\right|_{B}\Phi_{B}\left|\varphi^{\ast}\right\rangle_{B} (5.72)
=1d2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{2}}, (5.73)

from which the statement of the proposition follows by combining with the result of Proposition 21.  

Proposition 23

For a private state γA​B​A′​B′\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}} of log⁡d\log d private bits, the geometric squashed entanglement obeys the following bound:

EFsq​(A​A′,B​B′)γ≥log⁡d.E_{F}^{\operatorname{sq}}\left(AA^{\prime};BB^{\prime}\right)_{\gamma}\geq\log d. (5.74)

Proof. The proof is in a similar spirit to the proof of [Chr06, Proposition 4.19], but tailored to the fidelity of recovery quantity. Recall (3.4)-(3.7). Any extension γA​B​A′​B′​E\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}E} of a private state γA​B​A′​B′\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}} takes the form:

γA​B​A′​B′​E=UA​B​A′​B′​(ΦA​B⊗ρA′​B′​E)​UA​B​A′​B′†,\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}=U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}\left(\Phi_{AB}\otimes\rho_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\right)U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{{\dagger}}, (5.75)

where ρA′​B′​E\rho_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}E} is an extension of ρA′​B′\rho_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}. This is because the state ΦA​B\Phi_{AB} is not extendible. Then consider that

F​(A​A′;B​B′|E)γ=supℛF⁡(γA​B​A′​B′​E,ℛE→A​A′​E​(γB​B′​E)),F\left(AA^{\prime};BB^{\prime}|E\right)_{\gamma}=\sup_{\mathcal{R}}F\left(\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}E},\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AA^{\prime}E}\left(\gamma_{BB^{\prime}E}\right)\right), (5.76)

where ℛE→A​A′​E\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AA^{\prime}E} is a recovery map. From (3.4)-(3.7), we can write

γA​B​A′​B′​E=1d∑i,j|i⟩⟨j|A⊗|i⟩⟨j|B⊗VA′​B′iρA′​B′​E(VA′​B′j)†,\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i,j}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle j\right|_{A}\otimes\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle j\right|_{B}\otimes V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\rho_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\left(V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{j}\right)^{{\dagger}}, (5.77)

which implies that

γB​B′​E=1d∑i|i⟩⟨i|B⊗TrA^′{VA^′​B′iρA^′​B′​E(VA^′​B′i)†}.\gamma_{BB^{\prime}E}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle i\right|_{B}\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_{\hat{A}^{\prime}}\left\{V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\rho_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\left(V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\}. (5.78)

So then consider the fidelity of recovery for a particular recovery map ℛE→A​A′​E\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AA^{\prime}E}:

F⁡(γA​B​A′​B′​E,ℛE→A​A′​E​(γB​B′​E))\displaystyle F\left(\gamma_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}E},\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AA^{\prime}E}\left(\gamma_{BB^{\prime}E}\right)\right)
=F(UA​B​A′​B′(ΦA​B⊗ρA′​B′​E)UA​B​A′​B′†,1d∑i|i⟩⟨i|B⊗ℛE→A​A′​E(TrA^′{VA^′​B′iρA^′​B′​E(VA^′​B′i)†}))\displaystyle=F\left(U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}\left(\Phi_{AB}\otimes\rho_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\right)U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{{\dagger}},\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle i\right|_{B}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AA^{\prime}E}\left(\operatorname{Tr}_{\hat{A}^{\prime}}\left\{V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\rho_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\left(V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\}\right)\right) (5.79)
=F((ΦA​B⊗ρA′​B′​E),UA​B​A′​B′†[1d∑i|i⟩⟨i|B⊗ℛE→A​A′​E(TrA^′{VA^′​B′iρA^′​B′​E(VA^′​B′i)†})]UA​B​A′​B′),\displaystyle=F\left(\left(\Phi_{AB}\otimes\rho_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\right),U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{{\dagger}}\left[\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle i\right|_{B}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AA^{\prime}E}\left(\operatorname{Tr}_{\hat{A}^{\prime}}\left\{V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\rho_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\left(V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\}\right)\right]U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}\right), (5.80)

where the second equality follows from invariance of the fidelity under unitaries. Then consider that

UA​B​A′​B′†[1d∑i|i⟩⟨i|B⊗ℛE→A​A′​E(TrA^′{VA^′​B′iρA^′​B′​E(VA^′​B′i)†})]UA​B​A′​B′\displaystyle U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{{\dagger}}\left[\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle i\right|_{B}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AA^{\prime}E}\left(\operatorname{Tr}_{\hat{A}^{\prime}}\left\{V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\rho_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\left(V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\}\right)\right]U_{ABA^{\prime}B^{\prime}}
=(IA⊗∑j|j⟩⟨j|B⊗(VA′​B′j)†)[1d∑i|i⟩⟨i|B⊗ℛE→A​A′​E(TrA^′{VA^′​B′iρA^′​B′​E(VA^′​B′i)†})]×\displaystyle=\left(I_{A}\otimes\sum_{j}\left|j\right\rangle\left\langle j\right|_{B}\otimes\left(V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{j}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right)\left[\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle i\right|_{B}\otimes\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AA^{\prime}E}\left(\operatorname{Tr}_{\hat{A}^{\prime}}\left\{V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\rho_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\left(V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\}\right)\right]\times
(IA⊗∑j′|j′⟩⟨j′|B⊗VA′​B′j′)\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \left(I_{A}\otimes\sum_{j^{\prime}}\left|j^{\prime}\right\rangle\left\langle j^{\prime}\right|_{B}\otimes V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{j^{\prime}}\right) (5.81)
=1d∑i|i⟩⟨i|B⊗(VA′​B′i)†ℛE→A​A′​E(TrA^′{VA^′​B′iρA^′​B′​E(VA^′​B′i)†})VA′​B′i.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i}\left|i\right\rangle\left\langle i\right|_{B}\otimes\left(V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\right)^{{\dagger}}\mathcal{R}_{E\rightarrow AA^{\prime}E}\left(\operatorname{Tr}_{\hat{A}^{\prime}}\left\{V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\rho_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}\left(V_{\hat{A}^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}\right)^{{\dagger}}\right\}\right)V_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}^{i}. (5.82)
